Reference: Shapiro and Walker (2018)

Model Setting

Between 1990 and 2008, emissions of the most common air pollutants from US manufacturing fell by about 60 percent while real manufacturing output grew substantially. Three explanations are candidates: trade (dirty production moved abroad), environmental regulation (firms were required to abate), and productivity (fewer inputs per unit of output). The paper proceeds in two steps. First, a statistical decomposition with product-level data shows that almost all of the decline comes from lower emissions per unit of output within narrowly defined products (the technique effect), and not from the scale of output or the composition of products. Second, because pollution per unit of output is an endogenous outcome that any of the three forces could move, the paper builds a quantitative general equilibrium model that combines the heterogeneous-firm trade model of Melitz (2003) with the pollution abatement technology of Copeland and Taylor (2003). Firms choose abatement in response to a pollution tax, and entry, exit, production and exports all respond to regulation, productivity and trade costs.

The model is used to interpret the past and not to forecast. It delivers a closed-form expression for the implicit pollution tax, a scalar that summarizes the hundreds of overlapping command-and-control and cap-and-trade rules that firms face. It also allows a general equilibrium decomposition in which one shock at a time follows its historical path while the others are held at their 1990 values. The main findings are that the implicit pollution tax roughly doubled between 1990 and 2008 for the regulated (criteria) pollutants, with no increase for the unregulated pollutant carbon dioxide, and that this increase in regulatory stringency accounts for most of the decline in emissions. Foreign competitiveness, US productivity and trade costs, and shifts in expenditure shares account for little. The paper also provides the first estimate of the pollution elasticity that governs the trade-off between production and abatement.

Statistical Decomposition

Total manufacturing pollution ZZZ is the sum over products sss of product-level pollution zsz_szs​:

Z=∑szs=∑sxses=X∑sκses(1)Z=\sum_sz_s=\sum_sx_se_s=X\sum_s\kappa_se_s \tag{1}Z=s∑​zs​=s∑​xs​es​=Xs∑​κs​es​(1)

where xsx_sxs​ is the output of product sss, es≡zs/xse_s\equiv z_s/x_ses​≡zs​/xs​ is its emissions factor, XXX is total manufacturing output and κs≡xs/X\kappa_s\equiv x_s/Xκs​≡xs​/X is the output share of product sss. In vector notation Z=Xκ′eZ=X\kappa'\mathbf{e}Z=Xκ′e. Totally differentiating and dividing by ZZZ gives the scale, composition and technique effects:

dZZ=dXX⏟scale+dκκ⏟composition+dee⏟technique(2)\frac{dZ}{Z}=\underbrace{\frac{dX}{X}}_{\text{scale}}+\underbrace{\frac{d\kappa}{\kappa}}_{\text{composition}}+\underbrace{\frac{de}{e}}_{\text{technique}} \tag{2}ZdZ​=scaleXdX​​​+compositionκdκ​​​+techniqueede​​​(2)

Pollution comes from the National Emissions Inventory (NEI) of the Environmental Protection Agency, and output from the Census of Manufactures (CMF) and the Annual Survey of Manufactures (ASM), whose product trailer reports output for 1,440 five-digit SIC products (against 455 four-digit industries). The NEI is matched to the ASM in 1990 by name and address. Plant emissions are apportioned to products by revenue shares, and emissions intensities are fixed at their 1990 values, so that the decomposition shows what emissions would have been if only scale, or only scale and composition, had changed. Output is deflated with industry price indices from the NBER-CES database.

For nitrogen oxides, actual emissions fell by almost 50 percent. With 1990 emissions intensities, emissions would have risen by 20 to 30 percent, whether or not the product composition is allowed to change. Composition therefore changed little, and technique explains why emissions fell by 50 percent and did not rise by 30 percent. Other pollutants show the same pattern. The product-level decomposition gives almost the same answer as an industry-level decomposition of the kind used by Levinson (2009), and results are similar for single-product plants or when plant emissions are split equally among products. The decomposition is silent on the economic causes of the technique effect, which motivates the model.

Pollution Technology

Firms emit pollution according to:

zod,s(φ)=(1−a(φ))1/αsφlod,s(φ)(7)z_{od,s}(\varphi)=(1-a(\varphi))^{1/\alpha_s}\varphi l_{od,s}(\varphi) \tag{7}zod,s​(φ)=(1−a(φ))1/αs​φlod,s​(φ)(7)

where αs\alpha_sαs​ is the sector-specific pollution elasticity. Regulation is assumed stringent enough that all firms abate, and θs>(σs−1)(1−αs)\theta_s>(\sigma_s-1)(1-\alpha_s)θs​>(σs​−1)(1−αs​) is assumed so that expected profits are finite. This is the technology of Copeland and Taylor (2003) with firm productivity added. Solving for 1−a1-a1−a and substituting into the output equation shows that output is a Cobb-Douglas function of pollution and productive labor:

qod,s=(zod,s)αs(φlod,s)1−αs(8)q_{od,s}=\left(z_{od,s}\right)^{\alpha_s}\left(\varphi l_{od,s}\right)^{1-\alpha_s} \tag{8}qod,s​=(zod,s​)αs​(φlod,s​)1−αs​(8)

The parameter αs\alpha_sαs​ thus has three equivalent readings: the Cobb-Douglas share of pollution, that is, pollution tax payments as a share of production costs; the elasticity of emissions intensity with respect to abatement intensity; and the object that determines how pollution responds to productivity. Treating pollution as a taxed second output, as a priced input, or as a constraint are equivalent in this framework. The Cobb-Douglas form is essential: it delivers the first-order condition for abatement, which carries αs\alpha_sαs​ into every later result, and the regression used to estimate α\alphaα. The technology has constant returns in abatement; a model with fixed abatement costs would make prices depend on market size and would prevent the recovery of shocks described below.

In the competitive equilibrium consumers maximize utility, firms maximize profits, and labor supply equals labor demand in each country:

Lo=Loe+Lop+Lot+Lom+Lonx(9)L_o=L^e_o+L^p_o+L^t_o+L^m_o+L^{nx}_o \tag{9}Lo​=Loe​+Lop​+Lot​+Lom​+Lonx​(9)

More productive firms charge lower prices, so the pollution tax is larger relative to their output price and they abate more. Higher taxes shift labor to abatement. In the sector expression pollution taxes act directly through the denominator, while productivity and trade costs act through the price index Po,sP_{o,s}Po,s​: productivity growth raises real output per unit of pollution; lower iceberg costs mean that less output, and hence less pollution, is needed to deliver the same value; and lower fixed trade costs reallocate market share to more productive, cleaner firms (this last effect vanishes when θs=(1−αs)(σs−1)\theta_s=(1-\alpha_s)(\sigma_s-1)θs​=(1−αs​)(σs​−1), which shuts off firm heterogeneity). The trade effects scale with the openness term λdo,s\lambda_{do,s}λdo,s​, so they are limited for a relatively closed economy like the United States. The proposition is local and partial equilibrium, so any of the three forces could in principle explain the technique effect, and their magnitudes must be quantified.

Recovering the Historical Shocks

The decomposition needs the actual value of each shock in every year, denoted by an asterisk. Four shocks are recovered from country-by-sector data; a fifth shock to trade imbalances is needed to match the data exactly. Foreign competitiveness combines foreign productivity, foreign environmental regulation and foreign export costs, which need not be separated to study US pollution:

The first line is the definition; it is exactly the bundle that appears in the numerator and denominator of the free entry condition in changes. The second line is the measurement: the change in the share of destination expenditure that falls on goods from the foreign origin, adjusted for the changes in entry, wages, prices and expenditure. US competitiveness is the same bundle without the regulation term, which is separated because US emissions are observed:

Γ^od,s∗≡(1/b^o,s)−θs(τ^od,s)−θs/(1−αs)(f^od,s)1−θs/(σs−1)(1−αs),o=U.S.=t^o,sαsθs1−αsλ^od,sM^o,sew^o−θsP^d,s−θs1−αs(β^d,sw^dRd′−NX^dNXdRd−NXd)1−θs(σs−1)(1−αs)(21)\begin{aligned} \hat{\Gamma}^*_{od,s}&\equiv\left(1/\hat{b}_{o,s}\right)^{-\theta_s}\left(\hat{\tau}_{od,s}\right)^{-\theta_s/(1-\alpha_s)}\left(\hat{f}_{od,s}\right)^{1-\theta_s/(\sigma_s-1)(1-\alpha_s)},\qquad o=U.S.\\ &=\hat{t}_{o,s}^{\frac{\alpha_s\theta_s}{1-\alpha_s}}\frac{\hat{\lambda}_{od,s}}{\hat{M}^e_{o,s}\hat{w}_o^{-\theta_s}}\hat{P}_{d,s}^{-\frac{\theta_s}{1-\alpha_s}}\left(\frac{\hat{\beta}_{d,s}}{\hat{w}_d}\frac{R'_d-\widehat{NX}_dNX_d}{R_d-NX_d}\right)^{1-\frac{\theta_s}{(\sigma_s-1)(1-\alpha_s)}} \end{aligned} \tag{21}Γ^od,s∗​​≡(1/b^o,s​)−θs​(τ^od,s​)−θs​/(1−αs​)(f^​od,s​)1−θs​/(σs​−1)(1−αs​),o=U.S.=t^o,s1−αs​αs​θs​​​M^o,se​w^o−θs​​λ^od,s​​P^d,s−1−αs​θs​​​(w^d​β^​d,s​​Rd​−NXd​Rd′​−NXd​NXd​​)1−(σs​−1)(1−αs​)θs​​​(21)

It captures US productivity and export trade costs. Both competitiveness shocks are recovered separately for each sector and year, so a force that raises foreign competitiveness only in dirty sectors is captured. The expenditure share shock is the change in the Cobb-Douglas exponents:

β^d,s∗=∑oXod,s′/∑o,sXod,s′∑oXod,s/∑o,sXod,s(22)\hat{\beta}^*_{d,s}=\frac{\sum_oX'_{od,s}/\sum_{o,s}X'_{od,s}}{\sum_oX_{od,s}/\sum_{o,s}X_{od,s}} \tag{22}β^​d,s∗​=∑o​Xod,s​/∑o,s​Xod,s​∑o​Xod,s′​/∑o,s​Xod,s′​​(22)

It is a residual that lets the model reproduce observed sectoral expenditure. Finally, the shock to environmental regulation follows from inverting the sectoral pollution equation:

t^o,s=M^o,sew^oZ^o,s(23)\hat{t}_{o,s}=\frac{\hat{M}^e_{o,s}\hat{w}_o}{\hat{Z}_{o,s}} \tag{23}t^o,s​=Z^o,s​M^o,se​w^o​​(23)

The change in the implicit pollution tax equals the change in the mass of entrants times the change in the wage, divided by the change in emissions. Since free entry makes revenue proportional to wages times entry, the implicit tax is tied to the ratio of nominal revenue to emissions, while the technique effect of the statistical decomposition is Z^o,s/(R^o,s/P^o,s)\hat{Z}_{o,s}/(\hat{R}_{o,s}/\hat{P}_{o,s})Z^o,s​/(R^o,s​/P^o,s​), emissions per unit of real output. All three forces move the technique effect, but trade costs and productivity do so only through the price index P^o,s\hat{P}_{o,s}P^o,s​. When all shocks take their historical values the model reproduces the observed paths of emissions, production and trade.

Data

Parameters are estimated from plant-level microdata: the ASM of 1990 (about 60,000 establishments per year, used with sampling weights), the Pollution Abatement Costs and Expenditures (PACE) survey of 1990 and 2005, and the NEI. Counterfactuals use country-by-sector production and trade from the OECD Structural Analysis Database (1990-1995) and the World Input-Output Database (1995-2008), aggregated to two countries (the US and Foreign) and 17 manufacturing sectors (two-digit ISIC groups); intranational trade is production minus exports, and non-manufacturing is left out. US emissions come from the NEI in 1990, 1996, 1999, 2002, 2005 and 2008 for six pollutants: carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxides (NOx), particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Intermediate years are linearly interpolated.

Estimation of Parameters

Dividing the pollution technology by the output equation gives pollution intensity as a function of abatement:

zq=(1−a)(1−α)/α(24)\frac{z}{q}=(1-a)^{(1-\alpha)/\alpha} \tag{24}qz​=(1−a)(1−α)/α(24)

Taking logs and first differences Δ\DeltaΔ over time, and adding national trends ηt\eta_tηt​ and disturbances ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t}ϵi,t​:

Δln⁡(zi,tqi,t)=1−ααΔln⁡(1−ai,t)+ηt+ϵi,t(25)\Delta\ln\left(\frac{z_{i,t}}{q_{i,t}}\right)=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\Delta\ln\left(1-a_{i,t}\right)+\eta_t+\epsilon_{i,t} \tag{25}Δln(qi,t​zi,t​​)=α1−α​Δln(1−ai,t​)+ηt​+ϵi,t​(25)

where ai,ta_{i,t}ai,t​ is the abatement cost share of county-by-industry cell iii (six-digit NAICS) in year ttt. Abatement costs are endogenous: regulators make the dirtiest plants abate more (reverse causality, which biases (1−α)/α(1-\alpha)/\alpha(1−α)/α downward), the cost surveys contain measurement error, and regulation causes the dirtiest firms to exit. The abatement share is therefore instrumented with Clean Air Act nonattainment designations: the interaction of an indicator that the county switched into nonattainment between 1990 and 1993, after the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, with the share of the industry in national emissions of the pollutant in 1990. County-by-NAICS fixed effects are included and standard errors are clustered by commuting zone, with about 3,500 observations.

  • First stage: nonattainment lowers ln⁡(1−a)\ln(1-a)ln(1−a) in polluting industries, with coefficients from −0.057-0.057−0.057 to −0.126-0.126−0.126 across pollutants and −0.058-0.058−0.058 (0.009) for total emissions, so that regulated firms raise the cost share of abatement by about 6 percent of the baseline share. The first-stage F-statistic is 42 for the pooled regression, 14 for CO, 30 for NOx and 52 for VOCs, but only 1.4 and 3.4 for PM10 and PM2.5.

  • Reduced form and instrumental variables: the reduced-form coefficient on emissions intensity is negative for every pollutant and is −5.346-5.346−5.346 (1.979) for total emissions. The instrumental variables estimate of (1−α)/α(1-\alpha)/\alpha(1−α)/α is 91.604 (25.373) for total emissions and ranges from 58.6 to 130.0 across pollutants.

  • Pollution elasticity: the implied α\alphaα ranges from 0.008 to 0.017 across pollutants and is 0.011 (0.003) for total emissions. Firms behave as if they paid about 1 percent of production costs in pollution taxes, the same order of magnitude as reported abatement costs (about half a percent of manufacturing sales) and as the 2.6 percent productivity loss from nonattainment in Greenstone, List and Syverson (2012).

The sample is too small to run this regression by sector. Instead, because αs\alpha_sαs​ is the cost share of pollution taxes, if the tax rate is common across sectors then αs\alpha_sαs​ is proportional to tons of pollution per dollar of input costs. Relative values are measured this way and scaled so that the mean across sectors is 0.011. The resulting αs\alpha_sαs​ ranges from 0.0005 (radio, television, communication) to 0.0557 (basic metals), with 0.0303 for other non-metallic minerals, 0.0223 for paper and publishing, 0.0212 for coke and refined petroleum and 0.0205 for chemicals; these five sectors, with αs\alpha_sαs​ above 0.011, are labelled dirty and the other twelve clean.

The elasticity of substitution σs\sigma_sσs​ is obtained from the ratio of the value of shipments to production costs, which under monopolistic competition equals the markup. The estimates range from 2.89 (medical, precision and optical) to 8.18 (coke, refined petroleum), with a mean of 4.76. The Pareto shape parameter θs\theta_sθs​ comes from a regression of the log sales rank of a firm on its log sales in the 1990 ASM, following Hsieh and Ossa (2016) and Antras, Fort and Tintelnot (2017). The estimates range from 2.86 to 10.01 (basic metals), with a mean of 5.14 and a mean standard error of 0.23. They satisfy θs>(σs−1)(1−αs)\theta_s>(\sigma_s-1)(1-\alpha_s)θs​>(σs​−1)(1−αs​) in every sector. The exact estimating equations are in the online appendix.

The Implicit Pollution Tax

The recovered implicit tax on NOx nearly doubled between 1990 and 2008, and the rate of increase was similar for dirty and clean sectors. For the other criteria pollutants the increase was if anything faster: across pollutants, stringency rose by 75 to 250 percent. The interpretation is: if all regulation relevant to a pollutant were replaced by a pollution tax, what change in the tax would produce the observed firm behavior? The magnitude is plausible given the expansion of ozone nonattainment areas, the control requirements of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, the RECLAIM market in Los Angeles (1993), the Ozone Transport Commission market (1999) and the NOx Budget Trading Program (2003).

Two tests check that the recovered shock measures regulation. The first uses the NOx Budget Trading Program (NBP), a cap-and-trade market in the Eastern US that covered about 13 percent of manufacturing NOx emissions. With data aggregated by sector sss, region rrr (inside or outside the NBP area) and year ttt, the triple-difference regression is:

ln⁡(trst)=β1(1[NBPr]×1[NBPIndustrys]×1[Year>2002])+ηrt+γst+ψrs+ϵrst(26)\ln\left(t_{rst}\right)=\beta_1\left(\mathbf{1}\left[NBP_r\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[NBPIndustry_s\right]\times\mathbf{1}\left[Year>2002\right]\right)+\eta_{rt}+\gamma_{st}+\psi_{rs}+\epsilon_{rst} \tag{26}ln(trst​)=β1​(1[NBPr​]×1[NBPIndustrys​]×1[Year>2002])+ηrt​+γst​+ψrs​+ϵrst​(26)

with region-by-year, sector-by-year and region-by-sector fixed effects. The baseline estimate of β1\beta_1β1​ is 1.195 log points, an increase of about 230 percent in the implicit tax of regulated sectors in the NBP region. An event-study version shows no differential pre-trend and a sharp rise after the program starts. The second test recovers the implicit tax on carbon dioxide, which was essentially unregulated: it stays flat and if anything declines modestly, and manufacturing carbon dioxide emissions changed little.

Counterfactuals

Each counterfactual lets one shock follow its recovered historical path from 1990 to 2008 while the other shocks stay at their 1990 values, solves the two equilibrium conditions in changes for every year, and computes the implied emissions. All direct and indirect (general equilibrium) effects of a shock are attributed to that shock.

  • Foreign competitiveness: emissions would have risen by a few percentage points between 1990 and 2000 and then fallen modestly after 2000, when the growth of China accelerated, ending a few percent below the 1990 level. Chinese exports were concentrated in low-skill but not especially dirty sectors, the effect of China on US output was much smaller than on employment, and the statistical decomposition shows no shift in composition.

  • US competitiveness: between 1997 and 2003 this shock alone raised emissions by about 10 percent; afterwards it lowered them, but by much less than the observed decline. More productive plants are cleaner per unit of output, but with inelastic labor supply the factors that productivity growth frees are used to produce other output, so the technique effect is offset by a scale effect.

  • Expenditure shares: small decreases in emissions in the 1990s and an increase of 10 to 20 percent after 2000, as spending shifted towards pollution-intensive sectors.

  • Environmental regulation: regulation alone reproduces most of the observed decline of roughly 60 percent. In the early years it generates about 10 percent less reduction than actually occurred, and by 2008 it explains most of the change. The pattern is similar across the six pollutants.

Robustness and Extensions

Several exercises support the conclusion. First, the result is not built in: a counterfactual that doubles foreign competitiveness in a sector does lower the pollution intensity of that sector, as Proposition 1 predicts, but only by a few percentage points, because US import penetration is below 10 percent and because, in this class of models, the effects of trade on real income are themselves small (a 40 percent uniform global tariff lowers US GDP by less than 1 percent in Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare 2014). Second, shutting off firm heterogeneity by setting σs−1=θs/(1−αs)\sigma_s-1=\theta_s/(1-\alpha_s)σs​−1=θs​/(1−αs​) leaves the contribution of regulation nearly unchanged; the other shocks change more in magnitude but not in their qualitative role. Third, a partial equilibrium version holds wages and entry fixed, so that Z^o,s=1/t^o,s\hat{Z}_{o,s}=1/\hat{t}_{o,s}Z^o,s​=1/t^o,s​: regulation still lowers emissions substantially, and the other shocks have no effect by construction, so general equilibrium adjustments matter little for the conclusion about regulation. Fourth, removing φ\varphiφ from the pollution technology, so that pollution is proportional to inputs and not to output, changes the mechanism by which productivity affects pollution but yields identical expressions for emissions in the data and in counterfactuals. Fifth, the results are robust to alternative values of the Pareto shape parameter and the pollution elasticity and to adding a non-manufacturing sector (online appendix).

Limitations remain. The sector is the finest unit of the model, so offsetting within-sector changes in foreign competitiveness, or offshoring of dirty stages of production, are not captured; the product-level decomposition suggests that this is not of first order. Biased technical change towards cleaner inputs is unlikely to be the explanation, because the inputs that generate local pollutants also generate carbon dioxide, which did not fall. Markups are constant, and the response of markups to environmental policy is left for future work.

This is an accounting identity, not a behavioral equation. Total manufacturing pollution ZZZ (tons) is the sum of product-level pollution zsz_szs​. Each zsz_szs​ is written as output xsx_sxs​ (real dollars) times the emissions factor es≡zs/xse_s\equiv z_s/x_ses​≡zs​/xs​ (tons per real dollar), and output is written as total output X=∑sxsX=\sum_sx_sX=∑s​xs​ times the output share κs≡xs/X\kappa_s\equiv x_s/Xκs​≡xs​/X, with ∑sκs=1\sum_s\kappa_s=1∑s​κs​=1. In vector form:

Z=X κ′e,κ′e=∑sκses=ZXZ=X\,\kappa'\mathbf{e},\qquad \kappa'\mathbf{e}=\sum_s\kappa_se_s=\frac{Z}{X}Z=Xκ′e,κ′e=s∑​κs​es​=XZ​

so κ′e\kappa'\mathbf{e}κ′e is the average emissions intensity of manufacturing, an output-share-weighted mean of the product-level factors. The identity separates three objects that can move pollution: how much is produced (XXX), what is produced (κ\kappaκ), and how cleanly each product is produced (e\mathbf{e}e). It imposes no functional form; its only content is the level of aggregation sss. The paper uses 1,440 five-digit products so that shifts between clean and dirty products inside a four-digit industry are counted as composition and not as technique.

If XXX rises by 30 percent with κ\kappaκ and e\mathbf{e}e fixed, Z=260Z=260Z=260. This is the kind of counterfactual drawn in the paper: holding e\mathbf{e}e at 1990 values, emissions of nitrogen oxides would have risen by 20 to 30 percent, while they actually fell by about 50 percent. Composition lowers pollution only if output shares move towards products that are cleaner than average. What the form buys: a constant price elasticity σs\sigma_sσs​, hence a constant markup σs/(σs−1)\sigma_s/(\sigma_s-1)σs​/(σs​−1) (which is how σs\sigma_sσs​ is estimated from the ratio of sales to costs), and fixed sectoral expenditure shares, so that a shock in one sector reaches other sectors only through wages and total expenditure. The second line is the profit from one destination ddd: revenue, minus labor cost, minus pollution tax payments, minus the fixed cost fod,sf_{od,s}fod,s​ of selling in ddd.

This is the production function. A correction to the paper's text: the sentence after this equation in the paper states that regulation can be written as t^o,s=Z^o,s/R^o,s\hat{t}_{o,s}=\hat{Z}_{o,s}/\hat{R}_{o,s}t^o,s​=Z^o,s​/R^o,s​. The note's wording, that the implicit tax is tied to the ratio of nominal revenue to emissions, is the correct one.

Link to the statistical decomposition. The technique effect of a sector is the change in emissions per unit of real output:

Z^o,sR^o,s/P^o,s=P^o,st^o,s\frac{\hat{Z}_{o,s}}{\hat{R}_{o,s}/\hat{P}_{o,s}}=\frac{\hat{P}_{o,s}}{\hat{t}_{o,s}}R^o,s​/P^o,s​Z^o,s​​=t^o,s​P^o,s​​

It is the change in the sectoral intensity Io,sI_{o,s}Io,s​ of equation (11). Regulation lowers it through t^o,s\hat{t}_{o,s}t^o,s​, while productivity and trade costs lower it only through the price index P^o,s\hat{P}_{o,s}P^o,s​, as in equation (12). The measure attributes to regulation every change in emissions per dollar of revenue; it is an implicit tax in the sense that it summarizes all rules that make firms behave as if they faced that tax, and it would also pick up any other force that shifts the pollution share of costs, which is why the paper validates it with equation (26) and with carbon dioxide.

Take the pollution technology, equation (7), and the output equation (6), for the same firm and market:

z=(1−a)1/αφl,q=(1−a)φlz=(1-a)^{1/\alpha}\varphi l,\qquad q=(1-a)\varphi lz=(1−a)1/αφl,q=(1−a)φl

Divide the first by the second. Productivity and labor cancel, and the exponents of 1−a1-a1−a subtract:

zq=(1−a)1α−1=(1−a)(1−α)/α\frac{z}{q}=(1-a)^{\frac{1}{\alpha}-1}=(1-a)^{(1-\alpha)/\alpha}qz​=(1−a)α1​−1=(1−a)(1−α)/α

Emissions per unit of physical output depend only on the share of inputs devoted to abatement, with elasticity (1−α)/α(1-\alpha)/\alpha(1−α)/α with respect to 1−a1-a1−a. The relation is purely technological: it uses neither the first-order condition (13) nor any assumption about market structure, so it holds whatever the reason for the firm's choice of aaa (a tax, a standard, a permit price). This is what allows α\alphaα to be estimated without observing the tax. Because φ\varphiφ and lll cancel, productivity differences across plants do not confound the relation directly; they matter only through the choice of aaa.

Two remarks. First, a small α\alphaα corresponds to a large elasticity: a small change in the abatement share is associated with a large change in emissions intensity, so the estimate (1−α)/α≈92(1-\alpha)/\alpha\approx92(1−α)/α≈92 maps into α=1/(1+92)≈0.011\alpha=1/(1+92)\approx0.011α=1/(1+92)≈0.011. Second, in the data qqq is real output (deflated value of shipments) and aaa is measured by abatement costs as a share of total factor costs, the empirical counterpart of the share of labor assigned to abatement. Taking logs gives ln⁡(z/q)=1−ααln⁡(1−a)\ln(z/q)=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\ln(1-a)ln(z/q)=α1−α​ln(1−a), the basis of equation (25).

This is the estimating equation for the pollution elasticity. It is the log of equation (24), ln⁡(z/q)=1−ααln⁡(1−a)\ln(z/q)=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\ln(1-a)ln(z/q)=α1−α​ln(1−a), written in first differences over time for county-by-industry cell iii, with two additions: a national trend ηt\eta_tηt​ in emissions intensity and a disturbance ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t}ϵi,t​. The dependent variable is the change in log emissions per unit of real output; the regressor is the change in the log of one minus the abatement cost share; the coefficient is (1−α)/α(1-\alpha)/\alpha(1−α)/α, expected to be positive and large. First differencing removes any time-invariant cell characteristic, such as a permanently dirtier technology or a permanent measurement difference. The pollution elasticity is recovered as

α=11+ρ,ρ≡1−αα\alpha=\frac{1}{1+\rho},\qquad \rho\equiv\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}α=1+ρ1​,ρ≡α1−α​

with a standard error from the delta method; the estimate ρ=91.6\rho=91.6ρ=91.6 gives α=0.011\alpha=0.011α=0.011.

Identification. Ordinary least squares would be biased: regulators require the dirtiest plants to abate more (reverse causality), abatement costs are measured with error (attenuation), and regulation induces exit of dirty plants (selection). The paper instruments Δln⁡(1−ai,t)\Delta\ln(1-a_{i,t})Δln(1−ai,t​) with the interaction of an indicator for counties newly designated as nonattainment under the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments and the industry's share of national emissions of the pollutant. The variation is therefore the differential increase in abatement of polluting industries in newly regulated counties, relative to the same industries elsewhere and to clean industries in the same counties. The exclusion restriction is that nonattainment status changes emissions intensity only by changing abatement effort, and not, for instance, by changing the product mix within a cell. The ratio of the reduced form (−5.346-5.346−5.346) to the first stage (−0.058-0.058−0.058) gives the instrumental variables estimate, about 92.

The equation is estimated once for all manufacturing; sector-specific values αs\alpha_sαs​ are obtained by scaling with emissions per dollar of input costs, using the cost share interpretation of equation (8). The value of αs\alpha_sαs​ then enters every exponent of equations (15) to (21).

This regression tests whether the implicit pollution tax recovered from equation (23) responds to a known change in regulation, the NOx Budget Trading Program (NBP), a cap-and-trade market that started in 2003 in the Eastern United States. The dependent variable is the log of the implicit tax on nitrogen oxides, built from revenue, entry, wages and emissions aggregated to sector sss, region rrr (inside or outside the NBP area) and year ttt. The regressor is the triple interaction of an NBP-region indicator, an indicator for sectors with plants regulated by the NBP, and an indicator for years after 2002.

The fixed effects determine the comparison. Region-by-year effects ηrt\eta_{rt}ηrt​ absorb any shock common to all sectors of a region in a year (regional business cycles, other regional policies). Sector-by-year effects γst\gamma_{st}γst​ absorb national shocks to a sector (technology, demand, national regulation). Region-by-sector effects ψrs\psi_{rs}ψrs​ absorb permanent differences, including the unknown baseline level of the tax: since equation (23) identifies only proportional changes, the level of ln⁡(trst)\ln(t_{rst})ln(trst​) is arbitrary up to a cell-specific constant, and ψrs\psi_{rs}ψrs​ removes it. What remains is a triple difference: the change after 2002, for regulated relative to unregulated sectors, inside relative to outside the region. The identifying assumption is that no other shock hit regulated sectors in the NBP region after 2002; the event-study version checks for differential pre-trends.

The coefficient β1\beta_1β1​ is a difference in log points. The estimate 1.195 corresponds to

e1.195−1≈2.30e^{1.195}-1\approx2.30e1.195−1≈2.30

that is, an increase of about 230 percent in the implicit tax of regulated sectors in the region. By equation (19) with wages and entry fixed, this corresponds to emissions per dollar of revenue falling to about e−1.195≈0.30e^{-1.195}\approx0.30e−1.195≈0.30 of their previous level in those cells. The test is informative because the implicit tax is a model-based residual: any force that changes emissions per dollar of revenue is labelled regulation, so it is reassuring that the measure jumps where and when a real regulation begins, and that it stays flat for unregulated carbon dioxide.
